headline: Gituamba Girls Erupts as Urban Gang Tour Brings the Festival of Colours
dek: A full day of showcases, a runway, and a national broadcast turned GITCHEZ into the loudest school day of the term.
body: The sound reached the gate before the convoy did. By the time the Urban Gang Tour trucks rolled into Gituamba Girls High School — GITCHEZ, as the students say it — the compound was already humming, and by morning assembly it was clear this was not going to be an ordinary Cultural Day. It was going to be the day the whole term gets measured against.

The Festival of Colours ran wall to wall: stage and sound built to broadcast standard, mentorship pods running alongside the main programme, and a student body that refused to sit down from the first act to the final crowning.
## A Stage That Belonged to the Students

The talent competitions took everything the school had to give — music, dance, spoken word, comedy and modelling — and put it under real stage lights in front of real cameras. Girls who had only ever performed in classroom corners walked out to a full field and owned it. Some froze for a second at the size of the crowd. None of them froze twice.

Between performances, the mentorship pods pulled groups into focused sessions — careers, confidence, creative skills — the half of the tour that doesn't trend on the timeline but changes what a student believes she can do with her life.
> The loudest moment of the day wasn't a performance. It was the crowd screaming a classmate's name as she walked back to her seat, shaking, having just found out she could command a stage.
## The Runway and the Crown

The modelling runway, directed with Synapse Models, closed the day the way only a crowning can. Coached through cultural, creative and professional wear, the student models turned a school field into a fashion floor — and when the school administration crowned Miss of the Institution, the eruption could be heard past the fence line.

Hosts Eugine Micah and Lucy Ogunde anchored it all for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya — interviewing performers as they came off stage, pulling teachers in front of the camera, and making sure every category winner said her name, loudly, into a national microphone.
## Carried Far Beyond Kiambu

That is the part that outlasts the day: the feature aired nationally on Urban News, carrying Gituamba's name — and its students' names — far beyond Kiambu County. For one school day, GITCHEZ was national television. The posters come down; that doesn't.
Want your school's name said on national TV next? Bookings for the term are open — head to the booking page and lock a date before the calendar fills.

headline: Loreto Kiambu Girls Turns Out in Full Colour for the Urban Gang Tour
dek: The tour's June run opened at Loreto Kiambu with showcases, pods, and a runway finale.
body: Loreto Kiambu Girls High School has a reputation for doing things properly — and when the Urban Gang Tour arrived to open the June run, the school met a thirty-person production crew with a student body dressed, rehearsed and ready to compete.
This was the full production: stage, sound, lights and cameras, the same setup the tour carries to every stop, because a school day deserves the same standard as a headline show.
## A Programme With No Dead Air

Music, dance, spoken word and comedy showcases filled the day, students competing for their categories in front of judges and a crowd that treated every act like a final. The transitions were tight, the sets were short and loud, and the energy never dipped low enough to find a seat.

Between performances, the mentorship pods drew some of the biggest groups of the day — proof that the tour's promise is only half about the stage. Students packed sessions on careers, confidence and the creative economy, asking the kind of questions that don't fit inside a forty-minute lesson.
> The stage gets the noise. The pods get the notebooks out.
## Built for the Broadcast

Eugine Micah and Lucy Ogunde hosted throughout, stitching the day together on camera for a national Urban News feature on PPP TV Kenya. Every showcase, every pod, every crowning moment was captured — because at this tour, the school day and the television production are the same event.

The runway finale closed Loreto in full colour, and the June run was officially open. The bar was set high — and the next schools on the calendar heard about it before the trucks had even left the gate.
If your institution wants the full production — stage, mentorship, broadcast and all — the booking page is where it starts.

headline: Senior Chief Koinange Girls Kicks Off the 2026 Tour
dek: The 2026 second-term tour launched at Senior Chief Koinange Girls to a roaring crowd.
body: Every tour has a first stop, and first stops carry weight: they set the tone, the standard and the story for everything that follows. For the 2026 second-term run, that weight landed on Senior Chief Koinange Girls — and the school carried it like it had been rehearsing all year.
## MC Paps Lights the Fuse

MC Paps took the hall first, and warming up a crowd is a polite phrase for what actually happened. By the time the first performers stepped up, the hall was already at full volume — and it stayed there, act after act, all the way through to the final crowning.

The talent competitions ran the full spread — music, dance, spoken word, comedy, modelling — with students competing not just for judges' scores but for the roar of their own schoolmates. In a hall that loud, you learn fast who the crowd believes in.
> A season opener tells you everything. If Koinange was the preview, the term was going to be loud.
## Every Moment on Camera

Every moment was filmed for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya, giving Senior Chief Koinange Girls a national platform on day one of the season. For the students who performed, that means something specific: family in other counties watched them compete. Neighbours saw them crowned. Their school's name travelled.
The tour got the strong start a season needs, and the calendar filled up fast behind it. That's the Koinange effect — one loud day, and suddenly every school wants a date.
The 2026 run is still adding stops. If your school wants in, the booking page is open.

headline: Next Stop: Lari Boys High School as Bookings Stay Open
dek: The tour heads to Lari Boys High School in Kimende next, with more institutions still able to book this term.
body: The convoy's next destination is set: Lari Boys High School in Kimende, on 19 July. And if the pattern of this term holds, Lari is about to have the loudest school day in its history.

Preparations are already underway with the school administration to plan the day to the minute — because that is how the tour works. Nothing about a stop is improvised: the stage plot, the pod schedule, the competition running order and the broadcast plan are locked before the first truck moves.
## What Lari Should Expect

The full format travels: morning mentorship pods, tree planting on the school's own grounds, talent competitions across music, dance, spoken word and comedy, and the awards that close the day. All of it hosted by Eugine Micah and Lucy Ogunde, and all of it filmed for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya.

Boys' schools bring their own energy to the tour — a different kind of loud, heavy on the rap ciphers, the dance crews and the comedy sets that walk right up to the line. The crew knows it, plans for it, and frankly, looks forward to it.
> Every school thinks it's the loudest until the next one. Lari, the mic is about to be yours.
## The Calendar Is Still Open — For Now

Bookings for the remainder of the term remain open to schools, campuses and event organisers who want the full production and a national Urban News feature. But the calendar is a physical thing: there are only so many school days in a term, and each one can only belong to one institution.
Institutions can request a date through the tour's booking page. Tell us your date and your audience — we bring the stage, the mentors, the cameras and the crown.

headline: Ngeya Girls Locks In 24 July as Naivasha Gets Its First Stop
dek: The tour crosses into Nakuru County with a full production day confirmed for Ngeya Girls' Secondary School.
body: The Urban Gang Tour is officially leaving home. Ngeya Girls' Secondary School in Naivasha has confirmed 24 July for its stop — the first time the 2026 run crosses out of Kiambu County, and the first entry in what the crew is already calling the road-trip stretch of the season.
## Why This Stop Matters

A touring production proves itself the day it leaves its home county. Kiambu built the tour; Naivasha is where the 2026 run shows the format travels — that the same standard of stage, sound, mentorship and broadcast can land anywhere in the country and hit just as hard.

The full format makes the trip: morning mentorship pods, tree planting with Delo Greens on the school compound, talent competitions across every category, the Synapse Models runway, and a crowning to close the day — all filmed for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya.
> First stop outside Kiambu. Same stage, same standard, new county on the map.
## Naivasha, You're On National TV

For Ngeya's students, 24 July means their names, their performances and their school carried to a national audience. For Nakuru County, it means the tour map now includes you — and where the tour lands once, it tends to return.
Schools along the new route are already asking about dates. If yours is one of them, the booking page is the queue — and the queue is moving.

headline: St. Augustine Mlolongo Confirms 28 July — Machakos Joins the Map
dek: Four days after Naivasha, the convoy turns towards Machakos County.
body: The map keeps growing. St. Augustine Secondary School in Mlolongo has locked 28 July — four days after the Naivasha stop — stretching the second-term run across three counties and turning the back half of July into a genuine road tour.
## A Careers-First Brief

Every school shapes its own day, and St. Augustine's administration has been specific: a heavy careers focus in the mentorship pods. Digital literacy and creative-economy sessions are being lined up alongside the main stage — what a career in content, music, broadcasting or events actually looks like from the inside, taught by people currently living it.
It's a smart brief. Mlolongo sits on Nairobi's doorstep, its students close enough to the capital's creative economy to see it but rarely handed a map into it. On 28 July, the map comes to them.
> The stage shows students what they can do. The pods show them what they can become.
## And Then, the Show

The careers focus doesn't shrink the main event — the talent competitions, the showcases and the crowning all run at full scale, hosted by Eugine Micah and Lucy Ogunde and filmed for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya. St. Augustine gets the full production and the national broadcast that comes with it.
Three counties, one term, and the calendar still has room. If your institution wants a date — and its own brief — the booking page is open.

headline: Double Header in Maai Mahiu: Boys and Girls Editions Being Scheduled
dek: Two schools, one town — dates being finalised for late July and August.
body: The tour has done big days before. It has never done this: Maai Mahiu Boys and Maai Mahiu Girls are both on the calendar, dates being finalised for late July and August — back-to-back editions in one town, a first in the tour's history.
## One Town, Two Crowns

Each school gets its own full production day — its own stage, its own pods, its own competitions, its own crowning. Nothing is shared, nothing is halved. What is shared is the town, the bragging rights, and a storyline that writes itself.

Because make no mistake: both schools will be watching the other's day very closely. Whose crowd was louder? Whose performers went harder? Whose feature hit different when it aired on Urban News? The crew won't declare a winner. The town will.
> Two schools. One town. Everyone in Maai Mahiu is about to have an opinion.
## Watch This Space

Dates drop as soon as they're locked with both administrations, and Urban News on PPP TV Kenya will carry both editions nationally. Expect a cross-school rivalry storyline the whole country can follow.
Other towns with more than one school on the wishlist: the double-header format is now officially a thing. The booking page is where you make your case.

headline: Dr. Kiano Boys Enters the August Pipeline in Murang'a
dek: Githiga, Kangema is getting the full experience — the paperwork is moving.
body: Murang'a County, you're next on the list. Dr. Kiano Boys High School in Githiga, Kangema is in advanced planning for an August stop — which would take the Urban Gang Tour into its fourth county of the 2026 run.
## The School Is Already Rehearsing

Here's the detail that says everything about this stop: the paperwork isn't even final, and the school's drama and music clubs are already prepping entries for the talent competitions. That is what the tour has become — a date schools train for before it's even confirmed.

The clubs are right to start early. The competitions at every stop run at a standard that surprises first-time schools: real judges, real stage, real cameras, and a crowd that gives nothing away for free. The schools that shine are the ones that arrive rehearsed.
> The best sign a stop will be special: the students start preparing before the date is signed.
## The Full Experience, Kangema Edition

When the date locks, Githiga gets everything: morning mentorship pods, tree planting, the full competition programme, the runway, the crowning — and a national feature on Urban News on PPP TV Kenya, hosted by Eugine Micah and Lucy Ogunde.
August is filling in fast around this stop. Schools in Murang'a and beyond that want a date in the same window should get to the booking page while the window exists.

headline: Goshen Group of Schools and Achego Girls on the 2026 Radar
dek: Nakuru and Kisumu counties are calling — the wishlist keeps growing.
body: The clearest measure of the tour's momentum isn't the stops already played — it's the queue forming behind them. Two more names have entered booking conversations for third term: Goshen Group of Schools in Nakuru and Achego Girls in Muhoroni, Kisumu.
## The Map Keeps Stretching

Read those counties again. Nakuru — where Naivasha's Ngeya Girls already opened the door this term. And Kisumu — which would be the tour's deepest push west yet, taking the full production, the pods and the national broadcast to a region the 2026 run hasn't touched.

This is how the tour grows: one school hosts, the feature airs on Urban News, and then the calls start coming from schools two counties over asking how to get the same day. The wishlist doesn't shrink. It never has.
> Every feature that airs becomes an advert for the next school's ambition.
## A Word to Schools Still Deciding

Third term has a hard ceiling: a fixed number of school days, minus exams, minus closing weeks. Schools that want a 2026 date are being advised plainly — book now, because the calendar is filling fast, and January feels a lot further away when the school down the road just had its day on national television.
Goshen, Achego — the conversations are moving. Everyone else: the booking page is how you start yours.

headline: On The Mic: How Eugine Micah Turned a School Hall Into National Television
dek: The co-founder and lead host on building the loudest youth platform in the country.
body: Before the trucks, before the broadcast, before the crowns — there was a school hall, a microphone, and a conviction that young Kenyan talent didn't need to wait for permission to be seen. That conviction has a name: Eugine Micah, co-founder of the Urban Gang Tour and the first voice on the mic at every stop.
## From One Hall to a National Platform

What Eugine built, stop by stop, is unusual in Kenyan media: a travelling production that treats a school day with the seriousness of a headline show, then broadcasts it to the whole country. As lead host of Urban News on PPP TV Kenya, he turns every stop into television — carrying student names from a school field in Kiambu, Naivasha or Machakos into living rooms nationwide.

Watch him work a stop and the method shows. He learns performers' names before they walk on. He interviews the nervous ones first, so the camera catches them before the doubt does. He gives the crowd its moments but never lets the programme drift. It's showmanship in service of a schedule — the broadcast has to land, every single time.
> His rule for the crew is simple: the students are the stars; we are the amplifier.
## The Amplifier Principle

That rule — the students are the stars, we are the amplifier — is the whole architecture of the tour in one sentence. The stage, the sound, the pods, the runway, the cameras: all of it exists to make a sixteen-year-old's talent undeniable, first to her own school, then to the country.

Ask him what the platform is for and the answer is always the same: From Potential to Purpose. The mentorship pods carry the purpose half. The mic carries the potential half. Eugine carries both, every stop, all season.
You'll find him where you always find him — centre stage at the next stop, saying a student's name into a national microphone. Book the tour, and the next name he says could come from your school.

headline: Lucy Ogunde: The Voice Every School Trusts
dek: Co-founder, co-host, and the reason first-time performers dare to walk on stage.
body: Every production has a person the whole day quietly leans on. On the Urban Gang Tour, that person is Lucy Ogunde — co-founder, co-host of Urban News, and the reason a shaking first-time performer walks out on stage instead of backing out behind the curtain.
## The Moments Nobody Forgets

Lucy anchors the parts of the day that stay with people longest: the interviews where a student says her own name to a national camera for the first time, the pep talks behind the runway curtain, the crowning where a school's whole year of pride lands on one head. The loud parts of the tour make the noise; Lucy's parts make the memories.

Her range is the job. In one hour she can talk a nervous walker through her first runway steps, hold a live crowd through a set change, and land a broadcast segment clean enough to air untouched. Warmth that opens people up; authority that keeps the day on the rails.
> On camera she leads with warmth and lands with authority — which is why principals, parents and students all trust the tour with their biggest day.
## Why Trust Is the Whole Business

Think about what a school hands over when it books the tour: its students, its reputation, its one big day of the term. That trust has to be earned before the first truck arrives, and re-earned on camera all day long. Lucy is where that trust lives — the administrations know it, the parents feel it, and the students perform like it.

Co-founder, co-host, keeper of the tour's promise to every school it visits. When the next crowning airs on Urban News on PPP TV Kenya, watch who the newly-crowned runs to first. It tells you everything.
Want Lucy and the whole production at your school's biggest day? The booking page is open.

headline: Inside the Runway: Synapse Models and the Making of Mr & Miss
dek: How a T-shaped stage and a coaching squad turn first-time walkers into the stars of the term.
body: The crowning takes thirty seconds. The making of it takes days — and it belongs to Synapse Models, the coaching squad that turns students who have never modelled into the stars of the term.
## The Work Before the Walk

Every crowning starts long before the crowd arrives. Synapse Models and Head of Modelling Esther Wambui Gakunju coach student models through the full programme — cultural wear, creative wear, professional wear — teaching the walk, the turn, the pause, and the harder skill underneath all three: holding a stage while your whole school watches.

The transformation is the point. A student who signed up on a dare learns posture, presence and poise in a matter of days. The coaches will tell you the walk is the easy part; the belief is the work. By show time, both are ready.
> By the time the crown lands, the whole school knows every walker's name. That is the point.
## Thirty Seconds of Forever

Then comes the runway — the T-shaped stage, the lights, the categories, and a crowd that starts loud and gets louder. When the school administration crowns Mr and Miss of the Institution at the end of it, the eruption is unlike anything else on the tour. And it airs: every runway is filmed for Urban News on PPP TV Kenya.

For the walkers, the title outlasts the day — Miss of the Institution is a name a school remembers. For everyone watching, it's proof of the tour's core promise: give a student a real stage and real coaching, and watch what was hiding in plain sight.
The runway travels with every stop. Book the tour, and your school's first-ever Mr & Miss are already enrolled — they just don't know it yet.

headline: Two Decks, One Road: Carian & Xavi Keep the Tour Loud
dek: The XP Hub selectors reading every crowd from gate-open to pack-down.
body: There is a sound the Urban Gang Tour makes, and two people are responsible for it: DJ Carian and DJ Xavi, the selectors who keep a school field loud from gate-open to pack-down without ever once letting it go quiet.
## Reading the Room, All Day Long

A tour stop is a brutal DJ brief. The crowd's energy has to build all day and peak on cue, again and again: warm-up sets as students stream in, competition beds that lift performers without swallowing them, hype-set drops between segments, and the closing run that sends a whole school home buzzing. Carian and Xavi split the day between them and trade the pressure back and forth like a relay baton.

Watch them work and you see the craft: reading a crowd of teenagers in real time, knowing which track resets a dipping field and which one tips an already-wild one over the edge. It's not a playlist. It's a conversation with three thousand people at once.
> A school field at 2 PM should not sound like a Friday night headline show. On this tour, it does.
## The XP Hub Standard

Both selectors ride with The Experience Hub — the events engine behind the tour's biggest productions — and they bring that standard to every school stop: club-grade sound, broadcast-clean mixes, and a work rate that outlasts the crowd's. The same decks that run a campus rave run a school Cultural Day, at the same intensity.
That's the secret hiding inside the tour's sound: nothing is scaled down for a school audience. The students get the real thing, because they can tell the difference — everyone can.
Hear it for yourself at the next stop — or bring it to your own field. Tickets and bookings are both live on the site.

headline: Shot By Vibes: MC Dinjo's Studio Is the Tour's Eye
dek: The Vibe Studios joins as official photography partner — every iconic frame, theirs.
body: Every era of the tour will be remembered through somebody's lens. From now on, that lens belongs to The Vibe Studios — the outfit led by MC Dinjo, newly confirmed as the Urban Gang Tour's official photography partner.
## The Frames That Do the Travelling

The stills you see on the posters, the recaps, the gallery pages and this very article — those come out of The Vibe Studios' cameras. It's a bigger job than it sounds: a tour stop produces hundreds of moments an hour, and the photographs are what a school keeps after the stage comes down. Get them wrong and the day fades. Get them right and it becomes legend.

Dinjo's crew works a stop like documentarians, not event photographers. They're in the pods when a student asks the question that changes her plans. They're behind the runway curtain for the last deep breath before a first walk. They're at pit level when the crown lands.
> Their brief is one sentence: catch the moment a student realises the whole school is screaming their name.
## Why an Official Eye Matters

A travelling production that airs nationally needs its images to hit the same standard as its sound and stage — every stop, every county, no off days. That's what an official partner means: The Vibe Studios' frames now carry the tour's visual identity everywhere it goes, from the gallery on this site to the features on Urban News on PPP TV Kenya.
For the schools, there's a bonus baked in: your day gets shot by the same studio that shoots the whole tour. Your students' biggest moments, captured at national standard, in your own compound.
Browse the gallery to see the work — then imagine your school in the next set. The booking page makes that happen.

headline: One School, One Grove: The Delo Greens Tree Count Keeps Climbing
dek: Every stop leaves something growing — inside the students and on the compound.
body: The loudest day of the school year starts, at every single stop, with the quietest activity on the programme: students kneeling in the soil of their own compound, planting trees that will outlive everyone on the field.
## Hands in the Soil Before the Show

Straight after the morning mentorship pods, the Delo Green Movement — led by CEO King Tae (Justus Abuko) — takes over. Students plant on their own school grounds: holes dug, saplings set, names attached to trees. It's deliberate sequencing. Before the stage asks the students to be loud, the grove asks them to be responsible for something.

King Tae's crew doesn't run it as a photo opportunity. Students learn what they're planting, why those species, and who waters what after the trucks leave. The grove has owners, and the owners have names.
> Hands in the soil, names on the saplings — a legacy that will outlive every scoreboard.
## The Count Keeps Climbing

Every stop adds to the tally. School by school, the tour is leaving a chain of groves across the map it plays — Kiambu already, Nakuru and Machakos next, and every county the calendar reaches after that. Years from now, the surest evidence the Urban Gang Tour passed through a school won't be a poster or a hashtag. It will be shade.
It's also the quietest part of the tour's promise to administrations: we don't just take a day from your calendar, we leave something on your compound. Principals notice. Parents notice more.
One school, one grove — yours could be next. The tree planting travels with every booking, no extra ask. The booking page is open.

headline: The Heart at the Gate: How Moyo Response Keeps 3,000 Students Safe
dek: First aid stations, crowd sweeps and trained responders — the quiet department that lets the loud day happen.
body: The best-run department on the Urban Gang Tour is the one you're not supposed to notice. While the stage takes the cheers, Moyo Response — moyo is Swahili for heart — runs the quiet machinery that lets three thousand students be gloriously loud in safety.
## Gate-Open to Pack-Down

Moyo's cover starts before the first student arrives and ends after the last truck leaves: first aid stations placed and staffed, trained responders walking the crowd, sweep protocols between segments, and clear escalation lines to the nearest facilities. On-site emergency cover, all day, every stop — non-negotiable.

A tour stop is a dense, excited, all-day crowd of teenagers in the sun. Most days, Moyo's work is water, shade calls and the occasional twisted ankle. The point is what they're ready for — and that readiness is why the day gets to stay joyful.
> A safe crowd doesn't happen. It is staffed, planned and swept — by a team that treats a school field like a stadium.
## Duty of Care, in Writing

Here's what Moyo really gives the tour: the ability to promise schools a duty of care in writing, not just in spirit. When an administration hands over its students and its biggest day, that promise is what it's actually signing. Every parent asking 'but is it safe?' — Moyo Response is the answer, by name.
It's the least glamorous part of the production and the most important. The stage makes the tour famous. The heart at the gate makes it trusted.
Administrations planning a stop can request the full safety plan with any booking enquiry — it comes standard, like everything else that matters.

headline: The Roaming Mascot Has Entered the Chat
dek: An unnamed legend in a suit is stealing scenes at every stop — and nobody knows who is inside.
body: There is a new star on the Urban Gang Tour, and it has no name, no face and absolutely no shame. A mascot has started appearing at tour stops — and in the space of a few weeks it has gone from background gag to certified scene-stealer.
## The Charge Sheet So Far

The evidence is mounting: photobombing runway shots at the exact moment of the pose. Leading chants from the middle of crowds that did not invite it. Entering dance showcases uninvited and losing — deliberately, theatrically, unforgettably. Consoling eliminated contestants with hugs that last slightly too long. Every stop adds a new incident to the file.

The students, naturally, have adopted it completely. Mascot sightings get shrieked across school fields. Photos with it are currency. Its worst dance moves get replicated in the stands within minutes.
> The crew refuses to confirm who is inside the suit. The students have theories. Urban News is investigating.
## The Theories

And the theories are getting elaborate. It's a crew member on rotation, says one camp — explaining why the dance style changes between stops. It's the same person every time, insists another, citing a consistent signature wobble. A third faction claims the suit is occasionally empty, which raises more questions than it answers.

The crew's official position remains a shrug. The mascot's official position remains whatever pose ruins the next photograph. Urban News on PPP TV Kenya has opened an investigation it has no intention of concluding — some mysteries are worth more alive.
One thing is confirmed: the mascot travels with the tour. Which means the next school on the calendar should brief its photographers now. You've been warned.
